definition: Expressing sorrow or wistful longing for something that has been lost or has passed away.
example: The novel closes on an elegiac note, recalling summers at a family farm that was sold long ago.
nuance: Elegiac means mourning a particular loss, often in a dignified, lyrical way, while melancholy can be sadness with no clear cause.
prompt: A town band plays one last concert on an old pier the night before it is torn down.
options: The band's elegiac tune made the crowd remember every summer spent on the pier.
The pier's elegiac railings were carved with graceful, polished curves.
The elegiac polka was so bouncy and carefree that everyone laughed and danced.
The mayor gave an elegiac speech listing the demolition schedule and parking rules.
reasons: A tune that stirs sad memories of a place about to vanish fits the word's mournful tone.
Graceful design is elegance, a look-alike word; nothing here expresses grief.
Carefree cheer is the reverse of a lament for something lost.
A dry list of logistics carries no sorrow or longing at all.

practice.prompt: A photographer exhibits pictures of a fishing village whose residents have all moved away.
options: Critics called the frames elegiac because they were sleek, costly, and stylish.
The gallery's elegiac lighting meant visitors could easily read every caption.
Her elegiac photographs lingered on empty docks and faded boat names.
The elegiac photographs showed children splashing and grinning at a lively summer festival.
reasons: Sleek style describes elegance, not a sorrowful mood.
Bright, practical lighting has nothing to do with mourning.
Dwelling on abandoned, fading details mourns a way of life that is gone.
Joyful festival scenes celebrate the present instead of grieving a loss.
